Eggs, larvae, pupa, adults — the Anopheles way

blocks.x: Eggs: females lay 50–200 eggs directly on the water surface, one at a time. Dark brown to black, distinctively boat-shaped, with lateral air-filled floats for buoyancy — a key feature distinguishing them from other genera. Hatch in 2–3 days.

Larvae: 4 instars, ~7 days in the tropics (up to 14 in temperate regions). Unlike culicines, they lack a siphon and lie horizontally at the water surface, breathing via paired spiracles on segment 8. Segments 1–7 bear palmate hairs (float hairs); segments 1–8 carry tergal plates. They filter-feed and prefer clean, sunlit, unpolluted water.
Pupa: comma-shaped cephalothorax, 2 short respiratory trumpets, 8 visible abdominal segments with peg-like spines, paddles for swimming. Non-feeding; lasts 2–3 days in warm tropical conditions.

Adults: pale brown with wing veins bearing dark/pale scales in blocks; no scales on the abdomen (key vs. culicines); both sexes have long maxillary palps equal to the proboscis; rest at 45° or greater angle to the surface — a diagnostic field feature. Crepuscular to nocturnal.

sections.title: The Anopheles gambiae complex and other key vectors

blocks.x: The An. gambiae complex (sensu lato) comprises at least 8 morphologically near-identical sibling species differing critically in behaviour, breeding ecology, and geographic range — cryptic diversity with major implications for control.

items: An. gambiae s.s. — highly anthropophilic, primary sub-Saharan vector, freshwater breeder.
An. arabiensis — feeds on humans and animals, adapted to drier savanna.
An. coluzzii — highly anthropophilic, tends toward permanent water bodies.
An. stephensi — urban-adapted, container breeder, invasive, documented insecticide resistance.
An. melas — euryhaline, breeds in saline/brackish water (mangroves, tidal zones); secondary coastal vector.
An. funestus — highly anthropophilic, endophilic, long-lived, peak biting 10 PM–4 AM, breeds in permanent/semi-permanent vegetated water.

blocks.x: Because these species differ so much in behaviour despite near-identical morphology, molecular identification is essential for targeted control.

sections.title: The global and Ghanaian malaria burden

blocks.x: Anopheles are rightly called the "deadliest insect on Earth" — responsible for more human deaths than any other animal, through malaria, filariasis, and biting nuisance. Plasmodium spp. are transmitted exclusively by Anopheles.

Africa bears a disproportionate share: 94% of global malaria cases and 95% of global deaths occur in the WHO African Region (WHO 2023). In Ghana, P. falciparum — the deadliest species — causes about 90% of cases, and malaria accounts for roughly 30% of outpatient attendance and 20–25% of hospital admissions. Transmission is year-round but intensifies in the rainy seasons. Primary Ghanaian vectors: An. gambiae s.s., An. funestus, An. arabiensis.

sections.title: Plasmodium species, fever cycles, and transmission patterns

items: P. falciparum — malignant tertian, 48 hr cycle, most lethal.
P. vivax and P. ovale — benign tertian, 48 hr cycle, relapsing (dormant liver forms).
P. malariae — quartan, 72 hr cycle.
P. knowlesi — quotidian, 24 hr cycle, zoonotic.

blocks.x: Transmission patterns: holoendemic (year-round, very high constant intensity), hyperendemic (constantly high incidence), mesoendemic (seasonal), hypoendemic (low incidence, epidemic-prone).

The Plasmodium life cycle alternates between the human host (asexual liver and blood stages) and the Anopheles vector (sexual stages). Classic fever paroxysms — cold, hot, sweating stages — correspond to the synchronous rupture of infected red blood cells (schizogony).

sections.title: Why Anopheles is such an efficient malaria vector

blocks.x: Six traits combine to make Anopheles the world's deadliest disease vector:

items: Anthropophilic behaviour — strongly prefers human blood.
Endophagic & endophilic habits — feeds and rests indoors, repeated contact with sleeping humans.
High vector competence — physiology supports efficient parasite development midgut → salivary glands.
Longevity — a long adult lifespan is needed to survive the parasite's extrinsic incubation period.
Silent, stealthy feeding — nocturnal feeding on unaware, sleeping hosts.
Breeding adaptability — exploits diverse aquatic habitats, ensuring population resilience.

sections.title: Culicine mosquitoes: the larger, more diverse subfamily

blocks.x: Subfamily Culicinae contains 38 genera — far more diverse than Anophelinae — including Culex, Aedes, Mansonia, Sabethes, and Haemagogus. Major diseases: yellow fever, filariasis, and a wide spectrum of arboviruses.

Eggs lack Anopheles' lateral floats — each genus has its own oviposition strategy. Larvae: the most diagnostic feature is a siphon — a breathing tube on segment 8, absent in Anopheles — allowing larvae to hang at an angle below the surface. No tergal plates, no palmate hairs. Pupae: comma-shaped, long narrow respiratory trumpets, capable of diapause. Adults: rest parallel to the surface (vs. Anopheles' steep angle); females have abdominal scales (absent in Anopheles).

sections.title: Culex, Aedes, and Mansonia

blocks.x: Culex — eggs form a floating raft; larvae have a long narrow siphon, found in polluted stagnant water; adults bite at night, both endo/exophagic. C. pipiens fatigans — the "house mosquito" — is the primary filariasis vector. Diseases: avian malaria, West Nile, St. Louis Encephalitis, lymphatic filariasis.

Aedes — eggs laid singly, black with mosaic patterns, highly desiccation-resistant (diapause, viable for months). Larvae have a short barrel-shaped siphon. Adults show striking black-and-white silvery scales — a lyre-shaped thoracic marking in Ae. aegypti, banded "ringed" legs. Day-time biters, exophilic/exophagic. Diseases: yellow fever, dengue, Zika, chikungunya.

Mansonia — eggs in sticky rosette masses on leaf undersides; larvae pierce aquatic plants (e.g. water lettuce) with a sclerotized siphon and never surface — meaning standard surface larvicides are ineffective. Adults: large, dusty "pepper and salt" scale pattern, nocturnal, exophilic. Key vector of Wuchereria bancrofti.

sections.title: Mosquito-borne viruses: transmission dynamics

blocks.x: Arboviruses (arthropod-borne viruses) are naturally transmitted between vertebrate hosts and blood-feeding arthropods, with biological amplification occurring within the vector. Mosquitoes transmit roughly 72% of arboviruses globally — the most important vector group — followed by ixodid ticks (~18%).

Among mosquito genera, Culex transmits the greatest number of arboviruses, followed by Aedes, Anopheles, and Mansonia. Two transmission mechanisms: obligatory/biological (virus replicates within vector tissues — over 109 viruses transmitted this way) and mechanical (transferred on contaminated mouthparts without replication — ~402 viruses).

sections.title: Yellow fever: three transmission cycles

blocks.x: Caused by a Flavivirus — same genus as dengue, Zika, West Nile. A classic zoonosis maintained in forest monkey populations (Old World/cercopithecid monkeys), with humans as incidental dead-end hosts in the sylvatic cycle.

items: Cycle 1 — Sylvatic (jungle): maintained continuously among forest monkeys by Aedes africanus, a canopy-dwelling species.
Cycle 2 — Rural (intermediate): viremic monkeys forage near farms; the semi-domestic Aedes simpsoni bites them, then bites humans near the forest edge.
Cycle 3 — Urban: a viremic human travels to a city during their 3–4 day viraemic window; the domesticated Aedes aegypti bites and spreads the virus explosively through dense populations.

blocks.x: Virus multiplication in mosquito salivary glands (extrinsic incubation) takes 5–30 days. Transovarial transmission (mother to eggs) and transstadial transmission (persisting through larva → pupa → adult) let the virus persist across mosquito generations. In 2013, WHO estimated 127,000 cases with ~45,000 deaths.

sections.title: Dengue and the encephalitides

blocks.x: Dengue fever — "breakbone fever" for its severe joint/bone pain — is the world's most prevalent arboviral disease, ~400 million infections/year, transmitted primarily by Aedes aegypti and increasingly Ae. albopictus. Severe form: Dengue Haemorrhagic Fever (plasma leakage, thrombocytopenia).
St. Louis Encephalitis (SLE) — Flavivirus transmitted by Culex in the Americas; birds are the amplifying reservoir, humans are dead-end hosts.

Japanese Encephalitis (JEV) — leading cause of viral encephalitis in Asia (~68,000 cases/year, 20–30% case fatality); reservoir hosts are wading birds and pigs; primary vector Culex tritaeniorhynchus, breeding in rice paddies.

sections.title: Lymphatic filariasis: causative agents and periodicity

blocks.x: Caused by filarial nematode worms. Wuchereria bancrofti causes ~90% of cases (primary vector Culex quinquefasciatus, urban); Brugia malayi (South/SE Asia, Mansonia/Anopheles vectors); Brugia timori (restricted to Indonesia's Lesser Sunda Islands, An. barbirostris). Adult worms in lymphatic vessels block lymph flow, causing progressive lymphedema and, in severe cases, elephantiasis.

Microfilarial periodicity: nocturnal periodic (peak 10 PM–2 AM, matching Culex biting time), nocturnal subperiodic, diurnal periodic (Brugia malayi, day-biting Mansonia), and non-periodic. Inside the mosquito, larvae develop through two moults over 10–14 days to the infective L3 stage, deposited on skin during the next blood meal.

sections.title: Integrated Vector Management: "No vector, no disease"

blocks.x: <term d="Integrated Vector Management — the WHO-endorsed framework combining multiple control approaches to reduce vector-borne disease transmission.">IVM</term> is the WHO-endorsed strategic framework for reducing vector-borne disease transmission by combining multiple control approaches rationally. It is not a single intervention — it integrates all effective measures: chemical, biological, and environmental.

Core principles: evidence-based method selection, multiple interventions used together, cross-sector collaboration, community engagement, a robust regulatory framework, rational insecticide use, and good management practices.
IVM objectives: reduce breeding sites, reduce vector abundance and longevity, and reduce human-vector contact through behaviour change, physical barriers, and repellents.

sections.title: The IVM process: five cyclical stages

blocks.x: The IVM process is cyclical, not linear — monitoring and evaluation feed back into situation analysis and planning continuously.

items: Situation Analysis & Survey — baseline assessment: species identification, local ecology, insecticide resistance status, socioeconomic context.
Planning — epidemiological and vector assessment defining objectives, funding, and strategies.
Implementation — natural control factors (quarantine, biological/mechanical/physical/chemical control, sterilization, chemotherapy) deployed based on the situation analysis.
Monitoring — continuous data collection providing real-time feedback on program progress.
Evaluation — independent, in-depth assessment of program effectiveness, informing future decisions.

blocks.x: Community control is central: methods must be effective, affordable, simple, culturally acceptable, and safe. Housing, domestic vector ecology (breeding in-house, breeding on the body, adventitious insects), and self-protection tools (repellents, nets, vaporizers) round out the toolkit.

sections.title: Bringing it together

blocks.x: Anopheles and Culicine mosquitoes look superficially similar but differ in nearly everything that matters for disease transmission: resting angle, larval respiration, egg-laying strategy, and the pathogens they carry. Effective control depends on knowing exactly which genus and species you're dealing with — and deploying the right combination of tools through an Integrated Vector Management approach.
